youtube.title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning for One Second?
youtube.description:
You are having coffee in Paris when the ground stops spinning for one second. What happens to you, the air, the oceans, and what if it never restarted? We follow the physics from the cafe to the poles, then reveal the twist: Earth really is slowing down.

In this video:
- How fast are you moving right now?
- What would a sudden stop do to people, air and oceans?
- Where on Earth would you feel almost nothing?
- What if Earth never started spinning again?
- Why Earth is slowing down, and what leap seconds have to do with it

FAQ
Could Earth really stop spinning? No known process could do it suddenly. The spin only slows gradually, mainly through tidal friction with the Moon.
How fast does Earth spin? About 1,670 km/h at the equator, less at higher latitudes, near zero at the poles.
How fast is Earth slowing? The day lengthens by roughly 1.7 to 2.3 milliseconds per century.

Sources:
- NASA JPL, Gross et al.: 2011 Japan earthquake shortened Earth's day by about 1.8 microseconds
- Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016, 'Measurement of the Earth's rotation: 720 BC to AD 2015', Proc. R. Soc. A
- NASA, Lunar Laser Ranging: the Moon recedes about 3.8 cm per year
- IERS / BIPM: leap seconds since 1972; CGPM 2022 resolution to phase them out by 2035
- Mori et al. 2011, 'Survey of 2011 Tohoku earthquake tsunami inundation and run-up', Geophysical Research Letters
- NASA: Earth's magnetic field and the geodynamo

Which place would you pick for the one-second stop? Tell us in the comments.

scenes.text: Right now, you are riding a spinning planet at sixteen hundred kilometers an hour, and you feel nothing.
label: WHAT IF EARTH STOPPED?
For just one second

scenes.title: ONE SECOND
scenes.text: So what if Earth stopped spinning for just one second?
Everything attached to the ground would stop. Everything else would not.
label: THE RULE
Bolted down stops, the rest moves

scenes.text: You are having coffee in a European city, at about forty-nine degrees north.

scenes.title: 1,100 km/h
scenes.sub: Ground speed at Paris, 49 degrees N
scenes.text: Under your chair, the ground is sliding east at about eleven hundred kilometers an hour, just under the speed of sound.
You never notice, because the cup, the air, the street and you are all carried along together.

scenes.heading: WHICH WAY IS EAST?
scenes.question: Which way are you moving?

marks.text: FASTEST AT THE EQUATOR, ZERO AT THE POLES

scenes.text: With north at the top, the surface slides left to right, west to east, and so does everything on it. The speed depends on latitude: about sixteen hundred seventy kilometers an hour at the equator, falling toward zero at the poles.
scenes.fact: Equator: 40,075 km around,\Nturned once in about 24 hours.
scenes.teaser: THE STOP: WHAT HAPPENS TO YOU

scenes.text: Now, stop. The ground halts in an instant.
Your chair halts. The cafe floor halts. You do not.
label: THE GROUND STOPS
You do not

scenes.text: You keep going east at about three hundred meters per second, as anything does unless a force stops it.

hud.label: Your speed over the stopped ground

scenes.text: Skyscrapers and cafe walls are bolted to the ground, so they stop dead while you do not.
Buildings stay anchored. Anything unfixed, cars, furniture, people, would be thrown east, like debris in the worst tornadoes.
scenes.fact: Inertia: a moving object keeps moving\Nunless a force stops it.

scenes.text: And then there is the air. The atmosphere does not stop either.
label: THE ATMOSPHERE
Keeps moving

scenes.text: Relative to the stopped ground, it becomes a wind. Near the equator, that is about sixteen hundred seventy kilometers an hour.
That is faster than sound at sea level, and more than three times the fastest tornado wind ever measured.
Friction would slow the lowest layer, and exactly how much would reach the surface is uncertain, but the energy involved is enormous.
label: SURFACE FRICTION
Uncertain effect

scenes.text: From orbit, hurricanes look like slow, gentle spirals.
label: HURRICANES
Seen from orbit

scenes.text: They exist only because Earth spins: the Coriolis effect bends moving air into rotation.
scenes.fact: Hurricanes almost never form within\Nabout five degrees of the equator.

scenes.text: Without that spin, storms as we know them would fade away.
label: NO SPIN
No Coriolis effect

scenes.label: A STORM SPUN BY EARTH'S ROTATION
scenes.text: The same effect swirls this storm south of Iceland. Take the spin away, and the pattern goes with it.
The oceans keep going too. Water has huge inertia, and the whole ocean moves east with the seabed beneath it.
When the bottom stops, the water does not.
label: THE OCEAN
Keeps its speed

scenes.text: It would surge against west-facing coasts.
label: WEST-FACING COASTS
Hit first

scenes.text: Nobody can put an exact height on it, but the physics points to floods far beyond anything in recorded history.
label: FAR BEYOND
Anything recorded

scenes.text: For scale, the 2011 Tohoku tsunami sent floodwater through whole towns.
label: 2011 TOHOKU TSUNAMI
Real event, for scale

scenes.text: Its run-up reached about forty meters in places, and cars and debris were swept along.

scenes.question: Where would you feel almost nothing?
scenes.text: Quick test. Where on Earth would you feel almost nothing?
The North Pole. There, the ground simply turns on the spot once a day, so a researcher would barely notice a thing.
A Foucault pendulum shows the idea: at a pole, it swings in a fixed plane while Earth turns beneath it once a day.
label: FOUCAULT PENDULUM
Swings in a fixed plane

scenes.text: Anywhere else, its swing plane slowly appears to rotate, which is how it proves that Earth turns.
label: PROOF OF SPIN
Swing plane appears to turn

scenes.text: Now suppose the stop was permanent. Earth would still orbit the Sun, and every place would see the Sun rise once a year.
label: PERMANENT STOP
One sunrise a year

scenes.text: About six months of daylight, then six months of night.
scenes.fact: Stopped Earth: one sunrise\Nper year, not one per day.

scenes.text: The lit side would bake, and the night side would freeze.
label: DAY SIDE / NIGHT SIDE
Months-long extremes

scenes.text: Earth is not a perfect sphere: spinning gives it an equatorial bulge, about twenty-one kilometers.
scenes.fact: Equator bulges ~21 km: radius 6,378 km\Nvs 6,357 km at the poles.

scenes.title: OCEANS MIGRATE
scenes.text: Stop the spin and the oceans would slowly flow toward the poles, drowning high latitudes.
A broad belt of land would rise around the equator.
label: EQUATORIAL LAND
Exposed

scenes.text: And the magnetic field? Honestly, nobody knows for sure.
label: MAGNETIC FIELD
Honest answer: uncertain

scenes.text: Those field lines come from liquid iron churning in the outer core, a flow shaped by Earth's rotation.
scenes.code:
title=Text("INSIDE THE EARTH",font_size=40,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
crust=Circle(radius=2.6,color=GREY_B,fill_opacity=0.5,fill_color=GREY_D).shift(DOWN*0.3)
mantle=Circle(radius=2.0,color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=0.5,fill_color=ORANGE).shift(DOWN*0.3)
core=Circle(radius=1.2,color=RED,fill_opacity=0.7,fill_color=RED_E).shift(DOWN*0.3)
inner=Circle(radius=0.5,color=YELLOW,fill_opacity=1,fill_color=YELLOW).shift(DOWN*0.3)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(crust),Create(mantle),Create(core),FadeIn(inner),run_time=2)
arrows=VGroup()
for r in (0.8,1.0):
    for k in range(6):
        a=Arc(radius=r,start_angle=k*TAU/6,angle=0.8,color=YELLOW,stroke_width=5).add_tip(tip_length=0.18).shift(DOWN*0.3)
        arrows.add(a)
self.play(Create(arrows),run_time=1)
lab=Text("LIQUID IRON CHURNS",font_size=32,color=YELLOW).to_edge(DOWN)
l2=Text("crust",font_size=30,color=WHITE).move_to(RIGHT*4.5+UP*1.5)
self.play(FadeIn(lab),FadeIn(l2),Rotate(arrows,angle=TAU,about_point=DOWN*0.3,run_time=5,rate_func=linear))

scenes.text: If only the crust stopped, the core could keep stirring for a while. If the whole planet stopped, the field could weaken or change.
label: TWO CASES
Crust only vs whole planet

scenes.text: And with it, the shield that protects us from the solar wind and lights the auroras.
scenes.fact: The magnetic field shields us from\Nthe solar wind.
scenes.teaser: THE TWIST: EARTH IS ALREADY SLOWING

scenes.text: Here is the twist. Earth is slowing down, right now.
label: THE TWIST
Earth is slowing

scenes.text: The Moon's tides act like a brake, and the day grows longer by roughly one point seven to two point three milliseconds per century.
scenes.code:
title=Text("THE DAY IS GROWING",font_size=44,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
ax=Axes(x_range=[0,4,1],y_range=[0,3,1],x_length=9,y_length=3.6,axis_config={"color":GREY_B}).shift(DOWN*0.3)
xl=Text("time",font_size=30).next_to(ax,DOWN)
yl=Text("length of day",font_size=30).next_to(ax,LEFT).rotate(PI/2).shift(RIGHT*0.2)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(ax),FadeIn(xl),FadeIn(yl),run_time=1.5)
g=ax.plot(lambda x:0.8+0.45*x,x_range=[0,4],color=ORANGE,stroke_width=8)
self.play(Create(g),run_time=4)
t=Text("+1.7 to 2.3 ms per century",font_size=38,color=RED).move_to(UP*1.5+LEFT*1.5)
m=Text("the Moon's tides brake Earth",font_size=32,color=WHITE).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(t),FadeIn(m),run_time=1.5)
self.wait(1)

scenes.text: And the Moon itself drifts away from us.
scenes.fact: The Moon drifts away from Earth\Nabout 3.8 cm every year.
label: THE MOON
Drifting away

scenes.text: A thousand milliseconds, at under two a century: roughly fifty thousand years for the day to grow one full second longer.
Even earthquakes nudge it. In 2011, a huge earthquake struck Japan.
label: EARTHQUAKES
Can nudge the spin

scenes.text: NASA scientists calculated it shortened the day by about one point eight microseconds, by shifting Earth's mass closer to its axis.
That is why we have leap seconds. Atomic clocks keep perfect time. Earth does not.
label: LEAP SECONDS
Clocks vs Earth

scenes.text: Since 1972, timekeepers have added twenty-seven leap seconds, the last in 2016.
Lately Earth has even spun a little faster, and the world's measurement bodies voted to phase leap seconds out by 2035.
label: RECENT YEARS
Slightly faster

scenes.text: So the one-second stop never happens.
label: VERDICT
It never happens

scenes.text: Earth's spin holds hundreds of millions of years of humanity's energy use. Nothing known could remove it in a second.
label: SPIN ENERGY
Hundreds of millions of years of use

scenes.text: Instead, Earth gives up its spin in tiny, patient steps. Next time you sip your coffee, remember: you are on a ball turning at over a thousand kilometers an hour, and it is very slowly braking.
A one-second stop never happens. A day one second longer does, in about fifty thousand years.
label: THE REAL ENDING
Fifty thousand years

scenes.text: If this changed how you see your morning, subscribe. Every week, the strangest true science. Where would you want to be during the one-second stop? Tell me in the comments, and watch another video on screen.

shorts.title: You're Moving Up to 1,670 km/h Right Now

scenes.text: You are moving at up to sixteen hundred kilometers an hour right now, and you can't feel a thing.
label: UP TO 1,670 KM/H RIGHT NOW
And you feel nothing

scenes.text: That is how fast the equator is carried east as Earth turns once a day.
Stop the planet for one second, and the air keeps going: a supersonic wind.
Anything not bolted down keeps flying east.
But near the poles, where the ground barely moves, you would feel almost nothing.
The full story is on the channel, subscribe for the next one.
If Earth stopped for one second, the oceans would not stop.
label: THE OCEAN WOULD KEEP GOING
Even if the ground stopped

scenes.text: The whole ocean spins east with the seabed, at up to sixteen hundred kilometers an hour.
When the seabed stops, the water keeps going and floods west-facing coasts.
The 2011 Tohoku tsunami reached about forty meters in places.
A sudden stop could possibly bring a wave bigger than that.
The full story is on the channel, subscribe for the next one.
Your days are getting longer, and nothing can stop it.
label: EARTH IS SLOWING DOWN
Right now

scenes.text: The Moon's tides drag on Earth's spin, adding about two milliseconds to the day every century.
Four hundred million years ago, a day lasted about twenty-two hours.
And in 2011, one earthquake shortened the day by under two microseconds.
The full story is on the channel, subscribe for the next one.
